source_refs.note: Topic 5.14 with Example 5.5 and the Tidbits box (PDF 113, printed 110). Numerical 5.8's printed answer (9.90 m s^-1) does not follow from Eq. 5.31 for r = 0.5 mm; recorded as a finding.

blocks.text: Consider a water droplet such as that of fog falling vertically; the air drag on the droplet increases with speed. The droplet accelerates rapidly under the over-powering force of gravity, which pulls it rapidly downward; however, the upward drag force on it increases as the speed of the droplet increases. The net force on the droplet is net force = weight - drag force ... (5.29). As the speed continues to increase the drag force eventually approaches the weight in magnitude; finally, when the magnitude of the drag force equals the weight, the net force on the droplet is zero and the droplet falls with a constant speed called the terminal velocity.

blocks.title: Terminal velocity
blocks.text: To find the terminal velocity v_t we use Stokes' law for the drag force and equate it to the weight of the drop: 0 = m g - 6 pi eta r v_t, or v_t = m g / (6 pi eta r) ... (5.30). The mass of the droplet is rho V, where V = (4/3) pi r^3 is the volume of the sphere; substituting, v_t = 2 g r^2 rho / (9 eta) ... (5.31).

blocks.title: Example 5.5
blocks.text: A tiny water droplet of radius 0.010 cm descends through air from a high building. Calculate its terminal velocity, given eta for air = 19 x 10^-6 kg m^-1 s^-1 and the density of water rho = 1000 kg m^-3. Solution: r = 1.0 x 10^-4 m, rho = 1000 kg m^-3, eta = 19 x 10^-6 kg m^-1 s^-1. Putting the values in Eq. 5.31, v_t = 2 x 9.8 m s^-2 x (1.0 x 10^-4 m)^2 x 1000 kg m^-3 / (9 x 19 x 10^-6 kg m^-1 s^-1); terminal velocity = 1.1 m s^-1.
Parachutes increase air resistance (drag) by creating a large surface area, which counteracts the force of gravity; this slows down the person's fall, allowing them to land safely (Tidbits).
